result:
Solution 1 is the most likely to be correct. The check below is a heuristic calculation on the cycle, not a proof, and I have not confirmed it against the source paper.

**Cycle heuristic.** Take a single spike of height x at one vertex, so that a spike of size x occurs with probability about x^(-p) per vertex. This is allowed because the initial law may depend on n while keeping the L^p norm at most 1.

- On the cycle, mass spreads diffusively, so a spike of height x needs time about (x/ε)² to fall below ε. This holds for x up to about n, where the time reaches n².
- With n independent vertices, a spike of size x appears somewhere with probability about min(1, n·x^(-p)).
- Taking x = n^(1/p) gives a constant-probability spike and a time of order n^(2/p).
- For x between n^(1/p) and n, the expected contribution is about n·x^(-p)·x² = n·x^(2-p).
  - For p < 2 this increases in x, so it peaks at x ≈ n, giving n^(3-p).
  - For p > 2 it decreases in x, so the n^(2/p) term dominates.
- Larger spikes cost at most about n² times a log factor, but occur with probability only n·x^(-p), so they contribute less.
- The two exponents agree at p = 1 (value 2) and at p = 2 (value 1). Since 3 − p − 2/p = −(p−1)(p−2)/p, the exponent 3 − p is larger for 1 < p < 2 and 2/p is larger for p > 2. So β_p = max(2/p, 3 − p).

**Other solutions.**
- Solution 2 gives 2/p. It misses the heavier-tail regime 1 ≤ p < 2, where the rarer, larger spike of size about n gives the larger n^(3-p) contribution.
- Solution 3 gives 2. Its claim that i.i.d. ±1 initial data needs time n² log n on the cycle is wrong, because the i.i.d. fluctuations average out quickly. It also bounds only the typical case and ignores that the answer depends on p.

CHOICE: 1
